verses.text: Now when Adoni-Zedek king of Jerusalem heard how Joshua had taken Ai. and had utterly destroyed it; as he had done to Jericho and her king, so he had done to Ai and her king; and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel, and were among them.
They were very afraid, because Gibeon was a great city, as one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were mighty.
Therefore Adoni-Zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon, saying,
“Come up to me and help me. Let us strike Gibeon; for they have made peace with Joshua and with the children of Israel.”

Therefore the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered themselves together and went up, they and all their armies, and encamped against Gibeon, and made war against it.

The men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal, saying, “Don’t abandon your servants! Come up to us quickly and save us! Help us; for all the kings of the Amorites that dwell in the hill country have gathered together against us.”
So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he, and the whole army with him, including all the mighty men of valor.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Don’t fear them, for I have delivered them into your hands. Not a man of them will stand before you.”
Joshua therefore came to them suddenly. He marched from Gilgal all night.
Yahweh confused them before Israel. He killed them with a great slaughter at Gibeon, and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth Horon, and struck them to Azekah and to Makkedah.

As they fled from before Israel, while they were at the descent of Beth Horon, Yahweh hurled down great stones from the sky on them to Azekah, and they died. There were more who died from the hailstones than those whom the children of Israel killed with the sword.

Then Joshua spoke to Yahweh in the day when Yahweh delivered up the Amorites before the children of Israel. He said in the sight of Israel, “Sun, stand still on Gibeon! You, moon, stop in the valley of Aijalon!”

The sun stood still, and the moon stayed, until the nation had avenged themselves of their enemies. Isn’t this written in the book of Jashar? The sun stayed in the middle of the sky, and didn’t hurry to go down about a whole day.
There was no day like that before it or after it, that Yahweh listened to the voice of a man; for Yahweh fought for Israel.
Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp to Gilgal.
These five kings fled, and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah.
Joshua was told, saying, “The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah.”
Joshua said, “Roll large stones to cover the cave’s entrance, and set men by it to guard them;
but don’t stay there. Pursue your enemies, and attack them from the rear. Don’t allow them to enter into their cities; for Yahweh your God has delivered them into your hand.”
When Joshua and the children of Israel had finished killing them with a very great slaughter until they were consumed, and the remnant which remained of them had entered into the fortified cities,
all the people returned to the camp to Joshua at Makkedah in peace. None moved his tongue against any of the children of Israel.
Then Joshua said, “Open the cave entrance, and bring those five kings out of the cave to me.”
They did so, and brought those five kings out of the cave to him: the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.

When they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua called for all the men of Israel, and said to the chiefs of the men of war who went with him, “Come near. Put your feet on the necks of these kings.” They came near, and put their feet on their necks.
Joshua said to them, “Don’t be afraid, nor be dismayed. Be strong and courageous, for Yahweh will do this to all your enemies against whom you fight.”
Afterward Joshua struck them, put them to death, and hanged them on five trees. They were hanging on the trees until the evening.

At the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down off the trees, and threw them into the cave in which they had hidden themselves, and laid great stones on the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.

Joshua took Makkedah on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword, with its king. He utterly destroyed it and all the souls who were in it. He left no one remaining. He did to the king of Makkedah as he had done to the king of Jericho.
Joshua passed from Makkedah, and all Israel with him, to Libnah, and fought against Libnah.

Yahweh delivered it also, with its king, into the hand of Israel. He struck it with the edge of the sword, and all the souls who were in it. He left no one remaining in it. He did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho.
Joshua passed from Libnah, and all Israel with him, to Lachish, and encamped against it, and fought against it.

Yahweh delivered Lachish into the hand of Israel. He took it on the second day, and struck it with the edge of the sword, with all the souls who were in it, according to all that he had done to Libnah.
Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish; and Joshua struck him and his people, until he had left him no one remaining.
Joshua passed from Lachish, and all Israel with him, to Eglon; and they encamped against it fought against it.
They took it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. He utterly destroyed all the souls who were in it that day, according to all that he had done to Lachish.
Joshua went up from Eglon, and all Israel with him, to Hebron; and they fought against it.

They took it, and struck it with the edge of the sword, with its king and all its cities, and all the souls who were in it. He left no one remaining, according to all that he had done to Eglon; but he utterly destroyed it, and all the souls who were in it.
Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to Debir, and fought against it.

He took it, with its king and all its cities. They struck them with the edge of the sword, and utterly destroyed all the souls who were in it. He left no one remaining. As he had done to Hebron, so he did to Debir, and to its king; as he had done also to Libnah, and to its king.

So Joshua struck all the land, the hill country, the South, the lowland, the slopes, and all their kings. He left no one remaining, but he utterly destroyed all that breathed, as Yahweh, the God of Israel, commanded.
Joshua struck them from Kadesh Barnea even to Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, even to Gibeon.
Joshua took all these kings and their land at one time, because Yahweh, the God of Israel, fought for Israel.
Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp to Gilgal.

footnotes.content: When the news of Ai's destruction reached Adoni-Zedek, he understood the threat. The Lord was clearing a path for His people through the land, and no human fear could stand against His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear is a powerful teacher. The kings saw Gibeon's wisdom in making peace with Israel and understood their peril. When we see the Lord's hand at work, there's no hiding from the truth of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five kings from five cities—Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon—united by fear rather than true alliance. When people band together against the Lord's work, they're already lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Come help me" is how the world often speaks—recruiting others into its battles. But Gibeon's choice to side with Israel meant those kings were fighting not merely men, but the Lord Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five kingdoms combined their armies, yet none of them knew what Joshua knew: the Lord had already delivered the victory. Numbers and might mean nothing when the Lord has decided.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gibeon's cry—"Don't abandon us!"—is every faithful heart's prayer when surrounded by trouble. They knew their peace was with Israel because Israel's God is faithful. That faith is never misplaced.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua rose immediately with his full army, holding nothing back. That's what courage looks like—not the absence of fear, but obedience in the face of it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord's words to Joshua before battle: "Fear them not, for I have delivered them into thy hand." Past tense—already delivered. Before the fighting began, the victory was decided.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Marching all night from Gilgal shows Joshua's urgency. When the Lord calls us to action, delay honors neither Him nor those who are waiting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord "confused them"—He disoriented the Amorite armies, working both through Joshua's strategy and through His own hand. The greatest victories often come when the Lord confounds the plans of the proud.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hailstones from heaven killed more than the sword. The Lord Himself fought for Israel, using the very heavens as His weapon—a sign that He fights not only with earthly strength but with His sovereign power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Sun, stand still on Gibeon." Joshua's bold request echoes the faith of one who has seen the Lord's hand move. He asks for the impossible because he knows the Lord delights in faithful boldness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The sun stood still—a wonder that shattered the limits of the ordinary world. When the Lord is for His people, even the heavens obey. We serve a God who is Lord not just of armies but of creation itself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "There was no day like it before or after, that the Lord hearkened unto the voice of a man." This stands as unique in Scripture—a moment when the heavens themselves responded to a man's faithful prayer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After such wonders, Joshua and Israel returned to camp at Gilgal—to rest, to remember, to give thanks. The quietness after deliverance is where we really learn to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The five kings fled to a cave at Makkedah, seeking refuge in darkness. But there is no hiding place from the Lord. Caves become tombs when they become refuges from God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua was told of their hiding place. Nothing is hidden from the Lord, and He reveals what needs revealing to those who trust Him. The kings thought they were safe; they were merely delaying the inevitable.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua's command was precise: seal the cave and guard it. He left nothing to chance—wisdom is knowing both when to pray and when to act.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Pursue your enemies and strike them from behind. Don't allow them to enter their cities." Joshua understood that the moment of victory must be pressed—hesitation gives the enemy time to regroup.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Amorites were consumed—complete and thorough. Those few who made it to fortified cities did so as refugees, not conquerors. The Lord's victory was absolute.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "None moved his tongue against any of the children of Israel"—even in Israel's camp, no one dared speak against them. When the Lord has won the battle, the whole land knows it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua's command came after the battle was won, after the land had seen Israel's strength. Timing in mercy is part of Joshua's wisdom—he brings judgment, but he doesn't mock the fallen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The five kings—of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon—were brought before Joshua. Each had rallied their armies; each had chosen opposition to God's plan. Now they faced the account.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua called the soldiers near and said, "Put your feet on the necks of these kings." It was a sign—not of cruelty, but of complete submission and the end of opposition. The soldiers understood: the Lord had triumphed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Be strong and courageous, for the Lord will do this to all your enemies." Joshua's words were both reassurance and promise—what happened here would happen again and again. The Lord fights for His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua struck and killed the five kings, then hanged them as a sign. The harshness was the custom of war, but the meaning was clear: those who oppose the Lord's purposes meet His judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua commanded they be taken down at sunset and cast into the cave—returned to the place where they thought they were hidden. The cave that was meant to save them became their tomb, and his mark on it remains to this day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Makkedah fell on that day—complete destruction, nothing spared. Joshua's work was thorough because the Lord's command was clear: these cities must fall for His people to inhabit the land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Makkedah to Libnah—Joshua moved without pause. Each city in his path was another step toward the fulfillment of the Lord's promise to Abraham.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Libnah fell, and Joshua did to it as he had done to Jericho. The pattern was set: the Lord would deliver the cities, and Joshua would possess them for Israel. Consistency in obedience brings consistency in victory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To Lachish—one of the five cities whose king had banded against Israel. Now Joshua came to its gates. Sometimes the Lord allows us to see the fruit of our faithfulness almost immediately.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Lachish fell on the second day. Joshua's speed through these cities shows the Lord was indeed fighting, turning what might have taken months into a swift campaign of overwhelming force.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish, but Joshua met him and left no survivors. Even reinforcements could not stop the tide—the Lord's purpose moved forward like a flood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: To Eglon—another of the five kings' cities. Joshua came with the same certainty, the same strength. Each victory built the next; each city's fall made the next less likely to resist.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eglon was taken and destroyed in a day. By now, the cities themselves seemed to fall almost of their own weight before Joshua's approach. Fear does the conqueror's work before the battle even begins.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Up to Hebron—Hoham's city, another of the five kings. Joshua's campaign was complete in its scope, touching each of those who had conspired against Israel. None escaped.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hebron fell with its king and all its cities. Joshua spared none, leaving no resistance behind him. This completeness was not cruelty for its own sake, but the fulfillment of the Lord's will for the land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Hebron to Debir—the last of the major cities. Joshua's journey was nearly complete; the land was being won not by lingering battles but by the momentum of the Lord's hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Debir fell as all the rest had fallen. Joshua's work was methodical, relentless, and faithful. What began with a word from the Lord at Jericho was ending with the complete possession of the land.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua struck all the land—every region, every king—as the Lord commanded. Nothing was left breathing that opposed His purpose. This is how thoroughly the Lord keeps His covenants with His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Kadesh Barnea to Gaza, all the country of Goshen to Gibeon—Joshua's conquest covered the entire southern region. The scope was vast, yet accomplished swiftly because the Lord fought for Israel.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Joshua took all these kings and their land at one time, because the Lord, God of Israel, fought for Israel." The summary is clear: it was not Joshua's genius or Israel's strength, but the Lord's purpose fulfilled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua returned to Gilgal with all Israel—rest after victory, the promised land coming into possession. Readers today hear an echo in this: the promise of rest in the Lord, when all our battles are fought in faith and He carries us to the land He has prepared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
